questions.stem: What is Retrieval Recall in Information Retrieval and RAG, and how does it measure whether a search system finds relevant evidence?
options: Retrieval Recall measures the fraction of returned chunks judged relevant to a query. Higher recall therefore means fewer irrelevant passages are shown, even if many supporting passages remain undiscovered in the collection for every incoming query.

Retrieval Recall measures how often a language model produces an accurate answer after retrieval. Higher recall guarantees grounded responses even when the search system has missed several relevant evidence documents across heavily audited production RAG deployments.

Retrieval Recall measures the fraction of all known relevant documents or chunks that a retriever successfully returns. Higher recall means less relevant evidence is missed, but it does not guarantee that retrieved results are all useful.

Retrieval Recall measures the fraction of a model's indexed documents that appear in search results. Higher recall therefore means the retriever has explored more of the entire corpus, regardless of relevance labels across indexed search collections.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Recall asks, 'How much of the relevant evidence did we find?' If four documents are known to answer a question and search retrieves three of them, recall is 3/4 = 0.75. The denominator is all known relevant documents, not the number returned. In a RAG assistant, missing a critical policy section can prevent a complete answer. High recall helps evidence coverage, but irrelevant results can still distract the generator. Measure retrieval quality separately from final answer quality.

questions.stem: How is Recall@k calculated from a ranked result list, and how does its denominator differ from Precision@k and Hit@k?
options: Recall@k divides the number of relevant items found in the first k unique results by the total number of relevant items for that query. Precision@k divides by k, while Hit@k only checks whether any relevant item appears.

Recall@k divides the number of relevant items in the first k results by k, while Precision@k uses all relevant items as its denominator. Hit@k measures the position of the last relevant item under common retrieval evaluation settings.

Recall@k divides the number of all relevant items in the index by the number returned. Precision@k counts only missing relevant items, while Hit@k is the average number of relevant documents found across complete collections of user queries.

Recall@k divides the count of relevant items found in the first k results by all indexed documents. Precision@k uses the total relevant set, while Hit@k requires every relevant item to appear for each independently annotated search query.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Suppose five chunks are relevant to a question and the top three results contain two of them. Recall@3 is 2/5 = 0.40, but Precision@3 is 2/3 ≈ 0.67. Hit@3 is 1 because at least one relevant chunk was found. These metrics answer different questions: coverage, result concentration, and whether any evidence was retrieved. Use a fixed relevance unit, such as document IDs or chunk IDs, and count duplicate IDs only once in recall.

questions.stem: Why can increasing the retrieval cutoff k improve Recall@k while also increasing irrelevant context and RAG processing costs?
options: Increasing k always raises Recall@k by the same proportion because every additional rank must contain relevant evidence. The extra context is automatically useful, so prompt size and generation cost remain unchanged under every possible deployment.

Increasing k may reduce Recall@k because relevant items already retrieved become irrelevant at later ranks. Larger result lists therefore improve prompt efficiency by automatically removing earlier low-scoring evidence chunks across diverse independently annotated evaluation queries.

Increasing k changes the number of known relevant documents used as the recall denominator, so Recall@k can fall even when the exact same top-ranked evidence remains available in the output across multiple independent evaluation runs.

For a fixed ranked result list and relevance set, increasing k cannot reduce Recall@k because more candidate results are included. However, later results may be irrelevant, adding tokens, latency, and distraction to the RAG prompt.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Recall@k is based on a prefix of a ranked result list. Moving from top 3 to top 6 can find more relevant passages and cannot lower set-based recall for that fixed ranking. But the extra passages might be irrelevant, increase prompt tokens, or dilute the evidence the model should use. For example, a support assistant may recover a missing troubleshooting step at rank 5 while also retrieving two unrelated pages. Choose k using measured recall, latency, and context quality together.

questions.stem: How should a team construct ground-truth relevant evidence and a representative query set to evaluate Retrieval Recall reliably?
options: Create reference judgments automatically from the retrieval system's own highest-confidence results for evaluation queries, then assess that same retriever against those self-generated labels. This self-referential process supposedly guarantees exhaustive relevance coverage without human review.

Build held-out queries with clearly defined relevant document or chunk IDs, consistent annotation rules, and checks for incomplete labels. Evaluate representative query types, handle unanswerable questions separately, and avoid mixing document-level and chunk-level recall.

Label only the first document that supports each answer, even when several separate passages are necessary. Score chunk-level predictions against document-level IDs because the different evaluation granularity has no effect on the recall denominator.

Create evaluation queries entirely from training examples and treat every unanswered query as having zero recall. Missing relevance labels can be ignored because they cannot affect rigorous comparisons between retrievers with different ranking strategies.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Recall needs a reference set of relevant items for each query. Define what counts as relevant and whether the unit is a document, chunk, or supporting fact. For example, an insurance assistant may need two separate policy clauses to answer one question. Annotators should record both, review disagreements, and sample realistic queries. Missing labels can underestimate performance; evaluating a retriever on its own results introduces bias. A query with no relevant item has an undefined set-based denominator and should be assessed separately for answerability.

questions.stem: How can Python calculate Recall@k for retrieved document IDs, and why should evaluation avoid double-counting repeated IDs or silently scoring empty relevant sets?
options: Take the top-k retrieved IDs and divide the number matching any confidently indexed reference document by k. Keep repeated IDs as separate relevant hits, and assign a perfect recall score when ground-truth relevance labels are missing.

Take all retrieved IDs without actually applying k, then divide the number of repeated relevant hits by the number returned. Treat empty ground-truth sets as zero recall because no supporting documents were produced by the retriever.

Store unique ground-truth relevant IDs, take the top-k retrieved IDs, and divide the size of their set intersection by the ground-truth set size. Deduplicate matches and treat an empty relevant set as undefined or separately classified.

Take the top-k unique IDs, count every retrieved item as relevant, and divide by the index size. Ignore incomplete ground-truth annotations because exact document-ID matching does not depend on relevance judgments across realistic evaluated search queries.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A small Python function can compare the set of top-k retrieved document IDs with the labeled relevant-ID set. For example, if a query has four gold documents and the top three contain two distinct gold IDs, Recall@3 is 0.50. Repeating the same ID does not recover another relevant document. With no labeled relevant IDs, the denominator is zero: return an undefined value or track the query as unanswerable rather than inventing a score. The code below evaluates two example queries.

01 gold = {"q1": {"D2", "D4", "D7", "D9"}, "q2": {"D1", "D5"}}
02 ranked = {"q1": ["D2", "D8", "D7", "D3", "D4"],
03           "q2": ["D3", "D1", "D4", "D5", "D8"]}
04 def recall_at_k(results, relevant, k):
05     if not relevant:
06         return None  # no defined denominator
07     found = set(results[:k]) & set(relevant)
08     return len(found) / len(set(relevant))
09 for query, relevant in gold.items():
10     score = recall_at_k(ranked[query], relevant, 3)
11     print(query, f"Recall@3 = {score:.2f}")

Output: q1 Recall@3 = 0.50 and q2 Recall@3 = 0.50. Empty gold sets return None and should be reported separately.

Deduplicate relevant IDs and do not divide by zero for questions without known evidence.

questions.stem: How can embedding quality, chunking, metadata filters, hybrid search, and approximate nearest-neighbor indexes affect Retrieval Recall in a RAG pipeline?
options: Weak embeddings or poor chunk boundaries can bury relevant evidence, while restrictive filters can exclude it. Hybrid lexical-vector retrieval may improve coverage; approximate indexes can trade search accuracy for speed, so test recall against labeled relevance.

Embedding quality and chunk boundaries primarily affect generation fluency, not retrieved relevance. Once vector indexes are built, metadata filters cannot remove relevant documents, and hybrid retrieval only changes the order of identical candidates across production settings.

Hybrid lexical-vector retrieval guarantees perfect recall whenever either component finds a keyword match. Approximate nearest-neighbor search always returns the same top candidates as exact search, so index configuration affects latency only during real production search traffic.

Restrictive metadata filters can consistently improve recall by removing any document that does not match a preferred category, even if it contains necessary evidence. Larger chunks always preserve more relevant matches without harming ranking or attribution.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A relevant passage can be missed when its embedding poorly represents the query, a chunk splits key evidence, or metadata filtering excludes the right document. Hybrid search combines lexical and vector candidates, potentially recovering evidence missed by either. Approximate nearest-neighbor (ANN) indexes can trade exact-neighbor accuracy for speed. For example, a product-support RAG system may need both an exact model number and a semantic description. Measure labeled relevance recall end to end; ANN recall against exact neighbors is a different metric.

questions.stem: How should production RAG systems monitor Retrieval Recall across candidate generation, reranking, and final context selection while balancing answer quality and latency?
options: Measure recall only after answer generation because retrieval-stage labels no longer matter once a reranker is present. If generation quality is high on a small sample, candidate coverage and dropped evidence need no further monitoring.

Measure recall at the initial candidate pool, after reranking and truncation, and in the final context using the same labeled relevant evidence. Track latency, context budget, missing-evidence cases, and grounded answer quality alongside recall trends.

Measure initial candidate recall and assume a reranker preserves every relevant item when it selects a shorter list. Final context recall therefore equals candidate recall regardless of truncation, token limits, or duplicate handling under deployment.

Measure candidate recall, final answer fluency, and average latency, but avoid evaluating the selected context. Increasing the reranker score threshold always improves evidence coverage, even when relevant lower-ranked passages are removed under changing deployment workloads.
questions.explanation: Explanation: RAG retrieval has several gates: initial search, optional reranking, and the passages actually included in the model context. A relevant document absent from the candidate pool cannot be restored by reranking alone. Reranking can improve ordering, but truncating to a smaller context can drop evidence. For example, an internal policy assistant might find a required exception in the top 20 yet omit it from the final five chunks. Monitor Recall@20 and final Recall@5 with consistent labels, plus response faithfulness, p95 latency, and cost.
